en: Cannot be caught by the eye;
Your only one, whom you bore near death—
Whether he is dead or alive,
No one knows where he is.
When I follow the lore of tradition
And ask those who know,
He was your noble hero’s companion,
The sworn mate of his entrusted life;
When laid beneath him, he was his sure road,
When he rode for months, his countless host;
When foes made war, they shared the dust,
Shared one life and one death.
When climbing, he was his support,
The child of my bloodthirsty lord;
When riding to holy war, he was his swift steed,
The kinsman of the bloodthirsty lion.
Külchoro, left as a gift
By my champion father Albambet,
The wrestler and lion of the world,
Went boldly into single combat.
I heard that he was captured,
Caught in a net from which no bucking,
Startled creature could escape.
They say Kanchoro and brave Kyyaz
Took him alive;
They gouged his right shoulder,
Flayed him without mercy,
And reduced the falcon to this state.
They made Karagul, chief of the herdsmen,
Into a woodcutter;
They slaughtered the Sary-kan people,
And did every injury they knew
To my leopard uncle Bakay.
They say they plundered old uncle Bakay’s livestock
And feasted themselves;
The madmen made him a kökbörü ball
For forty wrestlers.
Mother, your thoughts must be troubled;
The child who drank your breast
Has brought overwhelming affliction.
Mother, did you see what I saw?
Did you learn what I know?
The pit already dug is coming,
The bitter brine already boiled is coming;
An immense, teeming army is coming.
White tasseled standards raise a tumult,
A tumult that splits the sky;
The massed black Jediger
Come as an overwhelming host.
Their champions are at the front,
Driving us into confinement and slaughter;
Mother, behind your son Kanchoro
Your senses have surely failed.
Firing arrows that embitter the soul,
They come flooding out—
Mother, the child who sucked your breast.
Look closely, mother, and see
That your child has become an enemy!
Pull crimson silk from the bias—
It will not part;
That madman struck by your breast milk
Shows no sign of turning toward us!
Pull green-mottled raw silk
From every side—it will not part;
When that good son of yours draws near,
He looks like one who will spare no life.
Breast milk has become mere dry curd;
When he grows fat, he raids your people.
Your footcloth is worthless as felt;
Breast milk has become dry curd no longer—
When he grows fat, he raids your people.
Your spring flowing from the hills,
Your brave son who sucked your breast—
Did your foster foal devour you?
When the time came to mount and ride,
Did he say he would be an equal brother?
Yesterday, on the plain of Jylgyndy,
Along broad Talas,
At Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
When the Kyrgyz lay spread across the land,
When Kanchoro, peerless in the world,
Was sucking your breast,
You did not heed every evil word;
You did not recognize his enmity.
This black-hearted choro
Will now fulfill to the end
The omen appointed for you.
My ash-gray foal, look closely:
He has drawn his bow like pouring rain;
Administer his punishment yourself.
He has struck without cease
The ninety thousand horses in the mountains;
Your ruinous Kanchoro
Raids your migrating camp from Keng-Köl.
To speak plainly, no male child remains—
How will you take your revenge?”
So Aychürök spoke,
Placing the blame before
Your dear mother Kanykey.
Then your champion mother Kanykey
Spoke softly but firmly,
And began a speech of many kinds:
“Ah, my foal, my child Aychürök,
What you have said is true!
Yesterday, when the forty choros were slain,
When they were killed for what they had done,
They joined together as enemies,
Raised a wicked quarrel,
Drew bows and fought;
When the forty choros became bitter foes,
Kambar took Kanchoro’s mother.
He wholly forgot his father
And became the son
Of that dark-hearted infidel,
The choro Kambar.
Calling him the brave son left by Chubak,
A legacy left by a noble man,
My champion son Semetey
Took him in as a gift.
When he came trotting over the lowland,
When my son brought him to me,
I took him under my protection.
So his heart might grow rich,
I cut him fat from the rump and fed him;
So he would be a brother without suspicion,
I nursed him with milk from my breast.
When Kanchoro drew and sucked
At my left breast,
My entire body trembled,
My fly-sized soul screamed,
And every bone in me ached.
With every suck, my strength departed;
Black blood flowed from my breast,
And strength left wretched me.
I understood, thinking carefully,
That in the end he would become an enemy,
That he would slaughter the people
Without leaving a single one.
I knew he would cast down black night,
Raid the people when he grew,
Grapple with us and plunge us into misery,
Learn our secrets and reach the root;
Kin on the outside, foul within,
He would bring us to this end—
I knew it long ago.
From the very beginning
I knew that deep down he was an enemy;
I always thought he would become our foe.
I tormented my fly-sized soul.
Agybay is here, Bakay Khan is here,
And all the many men
Who have exhausted nations and seen the world;
There are saints and heroes,
Sages whose sight encompasses
A journey of six months coming
And seven months going,
Whose eyes see from afar.
If all the peoples beneath moon and sky raced,
He would emerge alone from the contest.
His speech is renowned:
The old man, father of the people,
Who finds words in sudden peril,
Who finds eyes in the darkest night;
When he leads an army, none can bind him,
And in darkness, if set upon a corsac’s tracks,
He will never lose the trail.
There are elders skilled in hearing and knowing;
All this multitude is here.
While my grown son was here,
I raised a quarrel and would not nurse him.
I gathered the people into a nation,
Tirelessly brought them together,
And laid the matter before them,
Saying blood had flowed from my breast.
His face shows another nature;
In the end he bears an enemy's malice.
He will burn your wealth and cast you out;
In his malice he will destroy you.
He will turn your spirits to water,
Ruin your camp and fill it with clamor.
Instead of one wrong, he will do a thousand;
He is full of conflict, corrupt within.
This villain will break your power.
His mottled nature will never disappear;
His corrupt disposition will not mend.
His roots are black with malice;
That accursed enemy is full of venom.
If this companion of yours grows strong,
In the end he will become an enemy.
Gathering the champions, I cried out,
"Put out Kanchoro's eyes!"
For many days I sobbed.
When I spoke, my son would not obey;
When I lamented, he would not heed me.
Semetey, born a mighty beast,
Was perfect in every way;
The gray wolf's heart, if you could see it,
Was broader than a lake or river.
When his mother spoke, he glared;
He would not consent or care.
My words, spoken in lament,
He valued less than his boot-tip.
He refused to hear my words
And put me to shame.
He disregarded my counsel
And caused me bitter grief:
"The boy who is my support—
How can you tell me to seize and kill him?
Alas, Mother, what are you saying?
The companion who is my kinsman—
You tell me to seize and slaughter him outright!
He is only one unruly boy.
When a single boy proves wayward,
Unfortunate Mother, what are you saying?
Will the people panic and perch on rocks?
Will one lone boy become an enemy
And devour the whole world?
Will anyone prosper who sees
One infant child as a foe?
Black-hearted Mother, come to no good—
Can what you say be right?
Is there anyone who would slaughter
The nobleman's only hope?
Is there anyone who would kill
The khan's only son and support?
You are my mother in dark times,
My fortress above my head.
Do not twist a ruined affair;
Do not choke with rage, fierce Mother.
Do you mean to corrupt me?
Ah, my valiant, unfortunate mother,
How many monstrous words you speak!
How can I seize and slaughter
The boy who serves as my support?
How can we put to death
The kinsman who is our protection?
Unfortunate Mother, what are you saying?
Who knows whether the child in the cradle
Will one day become a lord?
Who knows whether the child in the womb
Will one day become a khan?
Saying you knew an unborn child
Would someday become an enemy,
My troubled, suffering mother,
You have spoken without reason.
When I climb, you are my support;
When I descend, you are the one I lean on.
Kanchoro and Kulchoro—
Both are my own younger kinsmen.
Almambet and Chubak are my two fathers;
These two are the legacy they left.
These heroes are like twins,
Lions who could shake the world.
With what face could I divide them?
These two youths whose names rhyme—
With what face could I part them?
